content: Carbon is composed of 8.9% carbon-12, which consists of 6 protons, 6 neutrons, and 6 electrons. Carbon-12 holds particular significance because it serves as the standard reference for measuring the atomic masses of all nuclides. By definition, its mass number is set at 12. Historically, prior to 1959, both the International Union of Pure and Applied Physics (IUPAP) and the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) used oxygen as the basis for defining the mole. Chemists defined the mole as the number of oxygen atoms that had a mass of 16 grams, while physicists used a similar definition but specifically referred to the oxygen-16 isotope. In 1959/1960, the two organizations reached an agreement to redefine the mole. This definition was subsequently adopted by the International Committee for Weights and Measures (CIPM) in 1967 and later by the 14th General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) in 1971. In 1980, the CIPM further clarified this definition, specifying that the carbon-12 atoms used in the standard are unbound and in their ground state.
